title: Least-Squares Regression
intro: Fit least-squares lines, interpret slope and intercept, and explain the coefficient of determination in context.

moments.title: Fit with technology
moments.text: Enter paired data and calculate the least-squares line.

moments.title: Least squares
moments.text: The fitted line minimizes the sum of squared vertical residuals.

moments.title: A point on the fitted line
moments.text: With an intercept, the least-squares line passes through the pair of sample means.

moments.title: Interpret slope
moments.text: Describe a predicted response change for each one-unit increase in x.

moments.title: Interpret intercept
moments.text: The intercept predicts the response at x=0 and may lack practical meaning.

moments.title: Coefficient of determination
moments.text: The squared correlation measures the proportion of response variation explained by the linear relationship.

moments.title: Fuel-efficiency example
moments.text: Interpret a negative slope in the original units.

moments.title: Recover the sign of r
moments.text: Take the square root of r squared and choose the sign from the slope.

cards.name: Least squares
cards.text: Minimize the sum of squared vertical residuals; the signed residual sum alone is not a measure of fit.

cards.name: Slope
cards.text: For each one-unit increase in x, the predicted response changes by b response units.

cards.name: Intercept
cards.text: The fitted response at x=0 may require extrapolation or be meaningless in context.

cards.name: Explained variation
cards.text: $r^2$ is the proportion of variation in the response explained by its linear relationship with the explanatory variable.

cards.name: Mean point
cards.text: A fitted least-squares line with an intercept passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$.

questions.q: The video models fuel efficiency in mpg from vehicle speed in mph, with slope −0.24 mpg per mph and $r^2=0.898$. Interpret the slope and explained variation, then find the correlation.

steps.t: Interpret the slope as a predicted rate of change.

work.text: For each additional 1 mph of speed, predicted fuel efficiency decreases by 0.24 mpg within the modeled range.
89.8% of the variation in fuel efficiency is explained by the linear relationship with speed.
Use the negative slope to choose the negative square root.

questions.answer: The linear association is negative, with correlation about -0.9476; 89.8% explained variation does not mean 89.8% of predictions are correct.

questions.obj: Fit a line and check its mean point
questions.q: Supplementary paired data: X=(5,7,12,16,20), Y=(16.5,18.9,19.1,21.6,25.7). Fit Y on X using least squares and identify the mean point.

work.text: Keep the observations paired and include an intercept.
Average the two lists separately while preserving their role in the regression.

steps.t: Check the fitted line at the mean input.

work.text: The unrounded fitted coefficients produce the mean response.

questions.answer: The fitted line passes through (12, 20.36), the pair of sample means.

sections.title: Desmos walkthrough
sections.intro: The calculator starts empty. Use the menus and controls below to carry out each task yourself, then reveal the expected result.

steps.title: Enter paired data
steps.suppose: we want a fitted line for the supplementary measurements.
do: Enter 5, 7, 12, 16, and 20 down the first column.
Enter 16.5, 18.9, 19.1, 21.6, and 25.7 down the second column in the matching rows.
Check that each row contains one original pair.
steps.observe: Use the same paired observations as the correlation example. Inspect the scatterplot for an approximately linear pattern.

steps.title: Fit the line through the table menu
steps.suppose: we want the least-squares prediction of the second column from the first.
do: On the table item, press [[Add Regression]] (the small line-and-points button).
Open the model selector if necessary and choose [[Linear Regression]].
steps.observe: The coefficient of the first-column variable is the slope; the constant term is the intercept. You do not need to type a regression equation using a tilde.

steps.title: Read explained variation
steps.suppose: we want correlation and its square.
do: Connect the sign of r to the fitted slope.
Express R-squared as a percentage when interpreting explained variation.
steps.observe: R-squared describes the proportion of variation in the response explained by its linear relationship with the explanatory variable.

traps.title: Slope without prediction
traps.weak: Every extra unit of x changes the actual y by exactly b.
traps.better: Interpret b as the change in predicted response for a one-unit increase in x.

traps.title: Explained variation versus accuracy
traps.weak: An r-squared of 0.898 means 89.8% of predictions are correct.
traps.better: It means 89.8% of the observed variation in the response is explained by the linear relationship.

traps.title: Lost correlation sign
traps.weak: The correlation is always the positive square root of r-squared.
traps.better: Choose the sign that matches the slope.

traps.title: Intercept always meaningful
traps.weak: The intercept always describes a realistic observation.
traps.better: It predicts y at x=0, which may fall outside the fitted range or be implausible.

notes.text: The CED includes calculating regression coefficients with technology. This page retains a calculator walkthrough even though parts of the video emphasize being given the equation.

questions.stem: For a linear regression with slope negative and r-squared 0.64, r is:
why: The sign must match the negative slope.
The magnitude is √0.64=0.8 with negative sign.
This has both the wrong sign and magnitude.

questions.stem: A model predicts mass from length and has r-squared 0.72. Which is the correct interpretation?
opts: 72% of variation in mass is explained by its linear relationship with length
72% of masses lie on the fitted line
why: This is not an accuracy rate for explanatory values.
It describes explained variation in the response.
Explained variation is not the fraction exactly on the line.

questions.stem: Which quantity does least squares minimize?
opts: The sum of squared vertical residuals
The signed sum of residuals alone
why: The input values do not change during fitting.
Balancing signs is not the fitting criterion.
Cancellation of signs can hide large errors.

questions.stem: A least-squares line with an intercept is fitted to data with mean x=10 and mean y=35. Which point is on it?
why: The mean y need not be the intercept.
The response at mean x is mean y.
The fitted line passes through the pair of sample means.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: A least-squares model predicts energy use in kWh from floor area in square meters: $\hat y=40+2.5x$, with $r^2=0.81$. The observed areas run from 20 to 150 square meters.
parts: (a) Interpret the slope and intercept, including any limitation on the intercept.
(b) Interpret r-squared and find the signed correlation.
(c) Predict energy use at 80 square meters and explain the least-squares fitting criterion.
sample: (a) For each additional square meter, predicted energy use increases by 2.5 kWh. The intercept predicts 40 kWh at zero area, but zero is outside the observed range and does not describe a realistic room here.
(b) 81% of the variation in energy use is explained by its linear relationship with floor area. The positive slope gives r=+√0.81=0.9.
(c) The prediction is 40+2.5(80)=240 kWh. The fitted line minimizes the sum of squared vertical differences between observed energy use and model predictions.
checklist: Interprets slope as a predicted rate with units.
Interprets the intercept and its contextual limitation.
Explains variation in the response rather than a prediction-accuracy rate.
Calculates 240 kWh and describes the least-squares criterion.
